v.why: Replacing a parameter-free skip edge with a 3x3 conv helps far more than replacing an edge that already carries a conv (e.g. +43 on C10 in the all-skip cell).
Cells with no learnable conv on this path gain a lot from a 3x3 conv, while conv-heavy cells gain little.
Swapping skip for a 3x3 conv adds capacity to a cell with little of it (+35 on C10 in the all-skip cell).
A direct input-to-output skip is replaced by a conv, which gives a large gain when the cell has few other convs.
The output-adjacent edge going from skip to a 3x3 conv gives the largest gain seen (+45 on C10 in the all-skip cell).
Turning a parameter-free skip edge into a conv helps much more than turning an already-conv or none edge into a 3x3 conv.
Removing a skip edge in a skip-dominated cell removes a harmful parameter-free path (+27 on C10), whereas removing a conv edge does not help.
Dropping a pooling edge from a pool-dominated cell helps (+15 on C10), unlike dropping a conv edge, which is neutral or harmful.
Replacing a 3x3 conv on the output edge with pooling discards learned capacity and hurts, most clearly on ImageNet16-120.
Replacing a pooling edge at the cell input with a 3x3 conv gives a large gain (+43 on C10 in the all-pool cell) compared with edits on conv edges.

raw:
These hypotheses come from the 100 measurements plus general NAS-Bench-201 behaviour. Most of the evidence comes from the single-op parents (all-skip and all-pool cells, rows 3, 4, 13, 14, 23, 24, 33, 34, 43, 44, 53, 54, 83, 84). In those cells, adding or removing an edge gives gains of 30 to 45 points on CIFAR. Mixed parents show much smaller effects, and some of them (for example rows 8, 17, 21 and 25) point the other way, so these are probable rather than certain.
